stops.name: Medina, chosen by lot for the campaign
stops.campa: Before the expedition against the Banu al-Mustaliq, the Messenger draws lots among his wives as he always does before a march, and the lot falls to Aishah. She rides in the curtained howdah tied to a camel led among the army's baggage, a young wife of thirteen going to war not to fight but simply because the arrow fell to her name. Nothing marks this departure as different from any other campaign; nothing warns the household of what the road home will bring upon her.

stops.name: Al-Muraysi, the campaign and the lost necklace
stops.campa: At the wells of al-Muraysi the campaign against the Banu al-Mustaliq is fought and won. On the march home, at a halt in the night, Aishah steps away from the camp to relieve herself and finds, on her return, that the onyx necklace borrowed from her sister Asma has slipped from her neck. She goes back into the dark to search for it while, unknowing that she is not inside her curtained litter, the men lift the empty howdah onto her camel and the army moves on without her.

stops.name: The desert behind the army, found by Safwan ibn al-Mu'attal
stops.campa: She finds the necklace, sits down where she is, and waits, certain the army will send someone back for her when they find her missing. Instead Safwan ibn al-Mu'attal, who had fallen behind the column overnight, comes upon her sleeping alone in the empty camp at dawn, recognizes her — he had seen her before the veil was ordered — and without a word kneels his camel for her to mount, leading it on foot the whole distance until they catch the army by full light of morning.

stops.name: Medina, the slander of Ibn Ubayy spreads
stops.campa: The sight of Aishah led into camp on a strange man's camel is seized on by Abdullah ibn Ubayy, chief of the hypocrites, who spreads through Medina the story that she has been unfaithful. Aishah, ill and unaware for nearly a month of what is being whispered against her, notices only that the Messenger's usual tenderness toward her has cooled; she asks leave to nurse her sickness at her mother's house and there, at last, another woman tells her plainly what all the city is now saying.

stops.name: Her father's house, the defense and the words of Jacob
stops.campa: Weeping until she thinks her liver will burst, Aishah hears the Messenger himself come to ask her, gently but plainly, to confess if she has done wrong, that God may forgive her. She answers that she will not confess to what she has not done, for he would not believe her innocence though God knows it, and takes for herself no words but those of Jacob when his sons brought him false news: patience is most fitting, and God alone is asked for help against what is said. Then she lies down and waits.
stops.quote: By Allah, I find no similitude for me and you except that of Joseph's father, when he said: So patience is most fitting, and it is Allah Whose help can be sought against that which you describe.
stops.quote_source: Sahih al-Bukhari 4141 (Aishah's own narration of the Ifk, echoing Quran 12:18)

stops.name: Medina, the revelation of An-Nur clears her name
stops.campa: As the household sits in silence the Messenger is overtaken by the state that comes upon him with revelation, sweating even in the cold, and when it lifts he is smiling. Glad tidings, Aishah — God has declared your innocence. Ten verses of Surah An-Nur come down naming the slander for what it is and setting the penalty for those who spread it. Her mother tells her to rise and thank the Messenger; Aishah answers that she will thank God alone, who has revealed her innocence from above the seven heavens.
stops.quote: Indeed, those who came with falsehood are a group among you... and the one who took upon himself the greater portion of it will have a great punishment.

stops.name: Sarif, the menses that interrupt the Farewell Pilgrimage
stops.campa: Six miles short of Mecca, on the Farewell Pilgrimage, her courses begin, and Aishah weeps, fearing she will be shut out of every rite of the Hajj she has waited years to make with him. The Messenger finds her weeping and tells her: this is a thing God has decreed for the daughters of Adam; do everything the other pilgrims do, only do not circle the House until you are pure again. So she completes the whole pilgrimage but for the one closed door, and is comforted.
stops.quote: This is a thing which Allah has ordained for the daughters of Adam. So do what all the pilgrims do with the exception of the Tawaf round the Ka'ba.

stops.name: Tan'im, the makeup Umrah granted to her alone
stops.campa: Still grieving that her Hajj feels incomplete beside her co-wives' full rites, Aishah is granted a concession found for no other pilgrim that year: her brother Abdur-Rahman rides her out to Tan'im, just beyond the sacred boundary, so she may enter a fresh state of pilgrim purity and perform a whole Umrah of her own before rejoining the caravan home. The small mosque later raised on that spot will carry her name into every century of pilgrims who pass through it on the same errand.

stops.name: Medina, his last illness, nursed in her own house
stops.campa: As the fever worsens the Messenger asks his other wives, one by one, where he is to be tomorrow, until they understand and grant him leave to be nursed in Aishah's room. He comes leaning on two men, his feet dragging the ground, and lies with his head in her lap. When the burning will not break he asks to be poured over with water from seven skins whose knots have not been loosed, so that he might rise and speak once more to the people gathered outside.
stops.quote: Pour on me seven water skins full of water, the tying ribbons of which have not been untied, so that I may give the people some advice.

stops.name: Medina, his death between her chest and chin
stops.campa: In the last hour he dips his hand in a vessel of water and passes it over his face, murmuring of the agony of death and the struggle of the soul's parting. Aishah holds him against her own body; his head grows heavy on her chest, his saliva mingles with hers from the toothstick they had shared, and between one breath and the stillness that follows, he is gone. She will say afterward that after that day she never again finds the death-agony of any other soul terrible to witness.
stops.quote: The Prophet died while he was between my chest and chin, so I never dislike the death agony for anyone after the Prophet.

stops.name: Medina, the grave dug beneath the floor of her room
stops.campa: Abu Bakr steadies the grieving city — whoever worshipped Muhammad, Muhammad is dead; whoever worships God, God lives and does not die — and the Companions recall the Messenger's own saying, that prophets are buried where they die. So the floor of Aishah's own small room is opened and he is laid in the earth beneath her feet, in the house she has lived in as his bride since she was a girl of nine. She goes on living beside the grave for the rest of her life, praying within arm's reach of him.

stops.name: Medina, widowed at eighteen, the household of grief
stops.campa: She is not yet twenty and already the Mother of the Believers, a title the Quran itself lays upon every wife of the Messenger, forbidding them ever to remarry. Her father Abu Bakr is chosen to lead the young community as its first Caliph, so that she watches the faith she was born inside pass from her husband's hands into her father's, still within the same small rooms by the mosque where she has always lived, now filling with visitors seeking counsel from both of them at once.
